summary: Foundational weather-naming topic for ages 5–7: children name and describe sunny, rainy, windy, snowy, cloudy, foggy and stormy weather, say what today's weather is like in simple words, and match weather types to symbols. Keep it concrete and observational — name the weather you can see and feel out of the window (looking at the sky and ground, never straight at the sun) — with no mechanism yet (that comes later). The core activity is a tap-to-reveal weather scene that attaches words and symbols to observable cues; strong follow-ons include a weather-report/tally builder (seeding patterns-over-time), matching/describe quizzes for checking vocabulary, and an optional weather-presenter conversation to elicit a child's own words.
misconceptions: 'It's a bad/good day' instead of a weather description — children conflate weather with mood/value; steer toward neutral descriptive words.
Cloudy vs foggy vs stormy blur together — distinguish by concrete cues (fog is low and you can't see far; storm has wind + rain + maybe thunder).
'Windy' is judged only by extreme gusts — gentle breezes count too; wind is a spectrum, not just gales.
Weather is only what's overhead now — children may miss that it changes through the day; the daily chart helps them notice.
Snow/ice only 'counts' as weather in storybook winters — include the full local range, and that some places rarely see snow at all.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal weather scene: name it and say how you can tell
steps: Look at one big, inviting weather picture (or a small set of them) showing several weather types at once.

Tap the blazing sun to reveal the word 'sunny', its symbol, and a lift-the-flap 'how can you tell?' that explains 'the sun is shining, the sky is bright and you can see shadows' (a sunny day can still feel cold).

Tap the falling rain to reveal 'rainy'; tap the trees bent sideways and the kite straining on its string to reveal 'windy'; tap the low white blanket you can't see through to reveal 'foggy'; tap the falling snowflakes to reveal 'snowy', the sky full of cloud to reveal 'cloudy', and the dark clouds with lightning and lashing rain to reveal 'stormy'.
For each revealed word, read the symbol shown in the activity's key alongside it (for example sun, cloud, raincloud, snowflake, wind lines, fog, storm) and say the word aloud.

In a 'what's it like today?' corner that mirrors a real class weather chart, look out of the window — at the sky and ground, never straight at the sun — then choose and place the symbol for today's actual weather.
activities.insight: Each weather type has a name, a symbol, and observable cues you can see or feel — and today's weather can be read directly from the sky and air.

activities.title: Sensory pairing: weather you feel as well as see
steps: Look at each weather image and pair it with a sense-word: sunny–bright (you may feel the sun on your skin, even on a cold day), snowy–cold, rainy–wet, windy–blowy.
Describe both what you can see and what it would feel like on your skin for today's weather.
Use sound and touch descriptions (the whoosh of wind, the patter of rain) to add to the weather word.
activities.insight: Weather is experienced through more than one sense — it is felt and heard as well as seen — which enriches the descriptive vocabulary.

activities.title: Build today's weather report and tally the week
steps: Drag weather symbols onto a simple map or report to 'build today's weather report'.
Over a week, add a symbol each day to a tally chart and count how many sunny, rainy or cloudy days there were.

Talk about which weather happened most across the week, and from looking out of the window recall that the weather can also change within a single day (e.g. sunny in the morning, rainy by the afternoon).
activities.insight: Weather recurs and changes over days — recording it with the same words and symbols lets you notice patterns over time — and it can also change within a single day.

activities.title: Match and describe: check the vocabulary
steps: Match each photo of real weather to the correct word and its symbol, going both ways (photo→word and symbol→word).
Choose which word best describes a shown scene (e.g. a grey overcast sky with nothing falling → 'cloudy').
Say what today's weather is in a full short sentence using the shared words.
activities.insight: Confirm that the weather words and symbols have stuck and can be applied to real conditions.

activities.title: Weather-reporter chat: say what it's like out there (optional)
steps: Pretend to be a weather reporter and tell a friendly presenter what the weather is like today.
Answer 'how can you tell?' by naming a cue you can see or feel.
Extend your own words when the presenter offers the matching shared weather word.
activities.insight: Children can produce weather descriptions in their own words, not just recognise them.

checkQuestion: Look outside (or at this picture): the sky is grey and full of clouds, but no rain is falling and the sun isn't out. Tell me what the weather is like right now, and how you can tell.
checkAnswer: It's cloudy (overcast). You can tell by looking at the sky — it's covered in grey clouds — even though nothing is falling and the sun isn't showing. Cloudy is a type of weather, just like sunny or rainy.
